The paper would be substantially strengthened by: (1) conducting multiple runs with different random seeds and reporting 95% confidence intervals for all metrics; (2) performing paired t-tests or permutation tests to assess statistical significance; (3) conducting ablation studies to explain concatenation advantage and isolate subjectivity effect from corpus size effect; (4) validating OpinionFinder accuracy on diverse corpora; (5) testing on modern architectures (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) and fine-tuning scenarios; (6) testing cross-lingual claims on multiple under-resourced languages with controlled confounds. The practical methodology (subjectivity filtering, concatenation) is the strongest contribution and could be emphasized more. The paper's contribution is primarily empirical-observational rather than theoretically grounded or conceptually disruptive. Recommend: (a) major revision addressing methodological gaps and providing mechanistic explanations, or (b) acceptance as a workshop paper or venue focused on practical NLP applications, with clear acknowledgment of limitations.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper addresses a practical problem in low-resource sentiment analysis and provides systematic empirical evidence for the utility of task-specific embeddings and subjectivity-based corpus filtering. The work is well-motivated and clearly presented. However, several critical gaps limit the impact and credibility of your findings: (1) **Statistical rigor**: Conduct multiple runs with different random seeds (5–10 runs) and report mean ± std dev or 95% confidence intervals for all metrics. Perform paired t-tests or permutation tests to assess statistical significance of differences between methods. This is essential for empirical claims. (2) **Mechanistic explanation**: Explain why concatenation outperforms appending/splicing through ablation studies (concatenation order, dimensionality allocation, alternative fusion methods) and representation space analysis. Quantify the subjectivity-quality correlation through regression analysis and test alternative corpus properties (domain vocabulary, sentiment lexicon density) as predictors. (3) **Confound isolation**: Conduct controlled experiments comparing subjectivity-filtered vs. random-filtered corpora of same size to isolate quality effect from quantity effect. Test concatenation with matched total dimensionality across all methods. (4) **Tool validation**: Validate OpinionFinder accuracy on diverse corpora through manual annotation. Compare to alternative subjectivity detection methods. For Catalan, validate tool on Catalan data or use language-specific classifier. (5) **Generalization**: Test on modern architectures (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) and fine-tuning scenarios, not just frozen embeddings with DAN. Evaluate on multiple under-resourced languages (Basque, Galician, Swahili, Tamil) with controlled corpus sizes and task types. (6) **Scope**: Expand evaluation to additional English datasets (SemEval, Twitter, product reviews) and related tasks (aspect-level sentiment, emotion detection). (7) **Clarity**: Revise overstated claims (e.g., 'always improve macro f1' contradicted by Table 2 OpeNER 50 dims). Discuss accuracy-F1 trade-offs explicitly. Acknowledge limitations of frozen embeddings and simple classifier architecture. (8) **Reproducibility**: Release code and detailed hyperparameters. Specify random seeds. Provide supplementary materials with additional results and error analysis. Your practical methodology is valuable for practitioners; emphasizing this contribution and providing honest discussion of limitations would strengthen the paper.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: The recursive deep models work in a bottom-top fashion over a parse-tree structure of a sentence to infer the sentiment label of the sentence as a composition of the sentiment expressed by its constituting parts: words and phrases. These models do not require any hand-crafted features or semantic knowledge, such as a list of negation words. However, they are computationally intensive and need substantial additional annotations (word and phrase-level sentiment labeling) to produce competitive results (Socher et al., 2013). top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. We analyzed the provided labeled data to determine why unigrams performed so strongly in the term-level task, and found that most of the test target tokens (85.1%) occur as target tokens in the training data. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.
